1. The population of the province 1. The GDP of the province

My proposal to determine the minimum wage would be doing (Province GDP / Province Population ) / 10. In some parts of Korea the minimum wage would rise and in other parts it would decrease. Income inequality, earning potential, and education are connected. The higher someone’s education, the more they’re likely to earn over a lifetime. The higher the earning potential, the less likely someone will be hurt by income inequality.

That’s why we hear many politicians, reformers, theorists, and those with particular philosophical axes to grind agree that people must attain higher levels of education for the economy to raor. Here are 2014 data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics that shows those with stronger education see lower rates of unemployment and higher incomes than the rest of the population.

Few will claim that more education is bad. Oh, many people don’t like sitting in a traditional classroom, and not everyone necessarily has the aptitudes for all areas of study. But a richer intellectual life and experience is a generally good thing. However, there’s a significant public policy mistake that happens when we move from “education is good” to “education will fix income inequality” or otherwise charge the economy.

Deeply embedded in that claim are three fundamental assumptions:

There is a way to pay for everyone going to college.

There is enough room in college for everyone to attend.There are enough jobs that make natural use of higher education.

Many people go through college with a combination of family money, grants, scholarships, and loans. But getting together the funds necessary to put everyone through college would be a political impossibility. Even funding free community college programs would be a major challenge.

However, say somehow that wasn’t a problem. We’d still face the lack of space in colleges. According to Census Bureau data, 41.4 percent of people 25 or older have a high school education or less. Another 16.7 percent have some college education but no degree. That leaves 41.9 percent with a degree, which could be anything from an associate’s to a doctorate.

We would have to more than double the education of people, getting virtually all through high school and then to at least a two-year associate’s degree. Given thelack of educational resources and overcrowding already happening at large public universities, it isn’t clear that the overall system could handle that many more students.

But say that it somehow could, perhaps through massive online courses (although they’d have to prove themselves). The third problem is the largest and most difficult: There aren’t enough better jobs requiring education available. Not even close.

Assuming for a moment that the higher paying jobs education is supposed to ready one for are the same as those that actually require higher education. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, two-thirds of all jobs in the country require a high school education or less:

Obviously there will be exceptions. A salesperson, for example, depending on the industry and native talent and drive might make a high income. An adjust university professor who pieces together work may long for even minimum wage. Still, on the whole, we assume a good income requires good education.

Unfortunately, we have nowhere near the necessary number of jobs to satisfy the population. There are areas that could absorb more qualified help if it were available, whether certain types of engineering or advanced manufacturing that needs specific skills for factory work. Those additional potential jobs are unlikely to equal twice the existing number of jobs that require college education.

It is fine to talk about education. Clearly many have, do, and will financially benefit from degrees (hopefully enough to pay those college loans). But ours is not on the whole a high-education labor market. And according to a 2013 study by University of Oxford researchers Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne, 47 percent of all jobs in the country could be replaced by automation within 20 years. A large portion of the jobs in danger are low-paying ones that don’t need additional education. How would the country handle that level of unemployment?

To really address the issue of jobs and economic inequality, we must start by acknowledging the reality of work and what more education can, and cannot, do. Solutions of any sort will need significant social changes. Perhaps as a country we forgo much of what automation could do. Maybe the answer is a higher minimum wage, recognition that many people will need income assistance, apprentice programs (maybe you’ll finally be able to find a plumber when the sink leaks before your dinner party), or even a considerable reduction in population over time. But chanting that education is the answer won’t fix anything.

**Daily Devotional**

**January 19**

*19 Then answered Jesus and said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise. (John 5:19 KJV)*

This scripture in no way is saying that Jesus was less than His Father, but is saying that they are one (John 17:21), and therefore the Son can do nothing but what the Father does. Some have tried to use this verse to say that Jesus was not God in the flesh, but was only a servant to God, and could do nothing on His own. Instead this is saying that Jesus and His Father were one, and operated identical to each other, so instead of it showing they are not equal, it shows that they were exactly the same.

Jesus was the exact copy of the Father (Hebrews 1:3), and if we look at what Jesus did while on the earth, then we can see exactly what the Father is like. Jesus cured, all those who would let him, of all illnesses and diseases as well as disabilities and all other maladies that the devil has put on us. He also cleansed the Lepers, cast out demons, and even raised the dead. If He is just like the Father, then how can some religious people say that it is not the will of God for us to do these things, as Jesus told us to do them (John 14:12)? God wants His children to be healthy, wealthy and wise, and will never put sickness or disease upon us (James 1:17), any more than Jesus did while on the earth. Praise God for His goodness, grace, mercy, and most of all His love.
